subject: Computer Networking
title: HTTP: The Language of the Web
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on HTTP: The Language of the Web.

hook.text: Every web page you've ever loaded was delivered by HTTP — the protocol browsers and servers share.

buildup.text: HTTP uses verbs: GET retrieves, POST submits, PUT replaces, DELETE removes. Clear and predictable.

discovery.text: Responses carry status codes: 200 means OK, 301 means moved, 404 means not found, 500 means server error.

twist.text: HTTP/1.1 opened one connection per request. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over a single connection.

climax.text: Despite being designed for documents, HTTP now carries APIs, video, games, and real-time data.

punchline.text: HTTP started simple. It became the web's universal language.

quiz.question: What does an HTTP GET request do?
options: Sends form data to a server
Deletes a resource on a server

details.summary: HTTP is a request-response protocol that defines how web browsers and servers communicate. Clients send requests with methods like GET and POST, and servers respond with status codes and content. HTTP is stateless, meaning each request is independent with no memory of previous interactions.
details.whyItMatters: HTTP carries virtually all web traffic and is the foundation of REST APIs, web applications, and microservice communication. Understanding HTTP is essential for any web development or networking role.
takeaways: HTTP uses request methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE
Status codes like 200, 404, and 500 indicate response outcomes
HTTP is stateless — each request is completely independent

faq.question: What are the most common HTTP methods?
faq.answer: GET retrieves resources without side effects. POST submits data to create resources. PUT updates resources by replacing them entirely. DELETE removes resources. PATCH makes partial updates. HEAD retrieves only response headers. These methods form the basis of RESTful API design.

faq.question: Why is HTTP stateless?
faq.answer: Each HTTP request contains all the information needed to process it, so servers do not need to remember previous requests. This simplifies server design and enables load balancing across many servers. Cookies, tokens, and sessions add statefulness on top of the stateless protocol when needed.
